content_voiceover: This slide defines classical PNH and its treatment algorithm, which is very testable. Classical PNH is diagnosed when the PNH clone exceeds thirty to fifty percent, plus symptomatic hemolysis with hemoglobin under seven to nine requiring transfusion, thromboembolism including any arterial clot or a venous clot with organ damage, or renal impairment with rising creatinine over two. Management splits into supportive care and anti-complement therapy. Supportive care includes folate and iron, leukoreduced transfusions, and meningococcal vaccination before starting a C5 inhibitor, since these patients risk meningococcal sepsis, plus pneumococcal and Hemophilus vaccines for proximal inhibitors. Full dose anticoagulation treats established thromboembolism, and prophylaxis is considered in high risk untreated patients. Anti-complement therapy includes terminal C5 inhibitors, eculizumab, ravulizumab, and crovalimab, which target intravascular hemolysis, and proximal inhibitors, pegcetacoplan against C3, and iptacopan or danicopan against the alternative pathway, which cover both intravascular and extravascular hemolysis. If anemia persists on a C5 inhibitor, think of four causes, underlying bone marrow failure, a C5 polymorphism causing resistance, breakthrough intravascular hemolysis from triggers or subtherapeutic levels, or extravascular hemolysis with a positive C3d DAT, which should prompt switching to proximal inhibition.
keypoints: Classical PNH: clone >30-50% + symptomatic hemolysis/thrombosis/renal impairment
Meningococcal vaccine mandatory before C5 inhibitors (± pneumococcal/HiB for proximal)
C5 inhibitors control IVH only; C3/proximal inhibitors control IVH + EVH
Residual anemia on C5i: marrow failure, C5 polymorphism, breakthrough IVH, or EVH (C3d+ DAT)
keypoint_voiceover: High yield board points here. Classical PNH treatment is triggered by a clone over thirty to fifty percent with symptomatic hemolysis, thromboembolism, or renal impairment. Always give meningococcal vaccination before starting a C5 inhibitor. Remember that C5 inhibitors only control intravascular hemolysis, while proximal C3 or alternative pathway inhibitors cover both intravascular and extravascular hemolysis. And if a patient has residual anemia on a C5 inhibitor, work through four causes, bone marrow failure, a C5 polymorphism, breakthrough intravascular hemolysis, or extravascular hemolysis marked by a positive C3d DAT.
